title: Eastward March
subtitle: Jaitugi of Devagiri and the Choice that Shaped the Eastern March
region: Devagiri and the Kakatiya country of Telangana
moral: Sometimes rule is secured by releasing an enemy wisely.

sources.citation: Hemadri, Chaturvarga Chintamani, dynastic praise sections
sources.note: Court account of the Kakatiya campaign, panegyrical and source-critical.

sources.citation: Garavapada inscription and early Ganapati Deva inscriptions
sources.note: Epigraphic anchors for the conflict and Yadava overlordship.

sources.citation: Cynthia Talbot, Precolonial India in Practice (2001); P.V.P. Sastry, History of the Kakatiyas (1978)
sources.note: Modern readings of Kakatiya-Yadava frontier evidence.

panels.shot: epic low-angle wide of a frontier landscape, Devagiri plateau fading west, distant Telangana plains east, with Jaitugi central between them

dialogue.text: Hemadri sings that Jaitugi crushed the Kakatiyas and chained Ganapati—yet he chose to free his captive and rule the eastern frontier through him. Why did a conqueror release his defeated enemy?

panels.shot: slow push-in on Jaitugi in council chamber at Devagiri, map-strewn stone floor

dialogue.text: In the late twelfth century, Devagiri’s Yadavas faced a harsh truth: the west was restless, the south uncertain, and the east—toward the Kakatiya country—lay half-known, yet full of rival claims and shifting loyalties.

panels.shot: wide bird's-eye over Deccan plateau showing multiple power centers marked by forts

dialogue.text: Yadavas at Devagiri, Hoysalas near Dorasamudra, and the rising Kakatiyas around Warangal watched one another across rugged lands. No border was neat; frontier was a living, contested space.

panels.shot: medium shot, Jaitugi listening intently to a messenger from the south

dialogue.text: Hemadri’s praise hints that Jaitugi first faced trouble on his southern flank, with Hoysala pressure near his borders. When that crisis ebbed, his attention turned, deliberately, toward the east.

panels.shot: close-up on Hemadri’s imagined hand writing with stylus on palm leaf beside an image of Jaitugi

dialogue.text: In his Chaturvarga Chintamani, Hemadri calls Jaitugi a lion who shattered the Kakatiya line, mentions a Raudra whose head was taken, and speaks of Ganapati seized like a captive elephant.

panels.shot: thoughtful close-up on Jaitugi’s face lit by lamplight, eyes turned toward the east-facing doorway

dialogue.text: Around 1191–1198 CE, he chose to march east. The campaign would test not only his force of arms, but the way Devagiri would hold its farthest lands.

panels.shot: epic wide of Yadava host moving east across rocky plains

dialogue.text: Columns of Yadava cavalry and infantry moved out from Devagiri. Their path led through dry uplands and river valleys toward the Kakatiya country, where hill-forts guarded the way.

panels.shot: tense wide of a Kakatiya hill-fort silhouette facing the approaching army

dialogue.text: Hemadri speaks of fort after fort subdued, a frontier pushed back. He names a Raudra fallen in battle, but the record stays silent on whether this was Rudradeva or Mahadeva.

panels.shot: dynamic mid-shot of Jaitugi in battle posture without showing gore

dialogue.text: The clash was fierce. Hemadri’s panegyric makes it blazing and absolute; modern scholars read through the praise to see a hard-fought border war, not an annihilated kingdom.

panels.shot: slow motion-like close-up of Ganapati being led bound but unharmed into Jaitugi’s presence

dialogue.text: From inscriptions and Hemadri’s words comes a stark image: Ganapati Deva taken captive. For a moment, the eastern frontier lay in Jaitugi’s hands, its chief prisoner before him.

panels.shot: intimate medium shot of Jaitugi and Ganapati seated opposite each other in a tent, guards outside

dialogue.speaker: jaitugi
dialogue.text: Rule your land, Ganapati—under Devagiri’s shadow, not against it.

panels.shot: wide shot of a palm-leaf treaty being placed between them, hands from both sides touching it

dialogue.text: The evidence is clear on the outcome: Ganapati ruled, but as a subordinate. Early Kakatiya inscriptions acknowledge Yadava overlordship, even as they continue to build local power.

panels.shot: high-angle shot of rugged Telangana countryside with scattered forts and villages

dialogue.text: Cynthia Talbot and P.V.P. Sastry read the frontier differently from Hemadri’s poems: the land was diverse, distant, and resistant to direct rule from Devagiri’s plateau.

panels.shot: medium shot of Jaitugi in council, advisers gesturing toward east on a map

dialogue.text: Jaitugi’s choice not to occupy Telangana directly was practical. Distance, terrain and limited manpower made vassalage—rather than full incorporation—the workable way to hold the frontier.

panels.shot: split-scene style: Devagiri court on one side, Ganapati’s court on the other, both functioning

dialogue.text: For some years, overlord and vassal coexisted: Yadava suzerainty above, Kakatiya authority below. The frontier was held not by Yadava administrators, but by a local ruler bound by obligation.

panels.shot: close-up of a Kakatiya inscription being chiselled, with the faint mention of Yadava overlordship

dialogue.text: Garavapada and other early Ganapati inscriptions speak of grants and titles under overlords. Through these dry lines of stone, the political compromise becomes visible.

panels.shot: wide shot over later Warangal fort, suggesting rising Kakatiya strength against distant Devagiri

dialogue.text: In time, Ganapati and his successors would grow stronger, challenging overlords old and new. Yet the memory of Yadava suzerainty marks an early phase of Kakatiya ascent.

panels.shot: reflective close-up on Jaitugi in older age, looking at both an unsheathed sword and a sealed document

dialogue.text: Hemadri remembers Jaitugi for the blow against the Kakatiyas. The frontier remembers him for something quieter: the decision to hold power with a released enemy, not a distant, strained occupation.

panels.shot: final wide shot of the Deccan from high above, borders invisible, routes and forts forming a web

dialogue.text: Jaitugi’s eastward march shows a frontier not as a line on a map, but as a living choice: when to advance, when to let another rule, and how power can rest on restraint as much as on conquest.
